source.title: Latxa: An Open Language Model and Evaluation Suite for Basque
source.authors: Julen Etxaniz; Oscar Sainz; Naiara Pérez; Itziar Aldabe; German Rigau; Eneko Agirre; Aitor Ormazabal; Mikel Artetxe; Aitor Soroa

record.tranche_reason: Tests the downstream-scaling version with a different measure: few-shot task accuracy across Latxa model sizes, rather than held-out pretraining loss or a fitted scaling law.
record.gate_note: The study reports downstream accuracy by model size. It does not report a parameter/token/compute power-law fit, small-run extrapolation, or a compute-optimal allocation sweep. Validation perplexity is described as tracked during training, but the text does not report a size-scaling result for it. Results cited from other studies are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: A model-release paper whose results include downstream few-shot accuracy at three parameter sizes (Llama 2 7B/13B/70B bases, each continued-pretrained on the same ~10B tokens). This bears weakly on V6, whether downstream performance improves with scale, in a new setting: continued pretraining for a low-resource language. No fit, extrapolation or loss–accuracy relation is reported, so the 'predictably' part is untested. T3 fits better than T2 because the study does not aim at the scaling question.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right, with one correction. The authors say larger Latxa models score substantially better: the 70B model is 10.99 points above 13B on average, and 13B is 9.14 above 7B. They frame this as going beyond 'conventional scaling laws' (Kaplan et al.), arguing that bigger base models help in continued pretraining despite limited target-language data. They do not fit or validate any predictive law.
record.recipe_differences: Continued pretraining of Llama 2 models on Basque data, evaluated with few-shot downstream accuracy; no held-out-loss scaling fit or compute-allocation sweep.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary by benchmark, although the Latxa scores increase across the three sizes for each Table 1 benchmark reported.

fits_no_version.finding: The gain from the same 10B-token Basque continued pretraining grows with base-model size: average gain over the Llama 2 base is +8.86 (7B), +15.84 (13B) and +25.19 (70B). The authors argue this contradicts a data-bottleneck reading of Kaplan et al.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In continued pretraining with a fixed, limited target-language corpus, the downstream benefit increases with the size of the base model.

record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (2024)
record.problems: Only three Latxa sizes are evaluated, and the evidence is downstream accuracy rather than held-out pretraining loss. No scaling-law fit, uncertainty estimates, or extrapolation test is reported.
record.rows_left_out: Detailed breakdowns are omitted: EusTrivia category scores in Table 5, BasqueGLUE task scores in Table 6, and EusExams category/test scores in Tables 12–13. These add task-specific downstream evaluations beyond the main Table 1 comparison; the response retains the main benchmark results and aggregate across all three sizes.

untested.parts: Whether downstream gains are predictable: no functional fit, no extrapolation, no relation to pretraining or validation loss. Only three sizes, with no uncertainty estimates.
Held-out loss vs parameters, tokens or compute. Validation perplexity is plotted (Fig. 1) but not analysed by size.
No loss power law is measured for continued pretraining.

missing.what: Per-task BasqueGLUE scores across Latxa sizes, showing non-monotonic scaling: BEC 57.30/53.92/61.06, BHTC 57.44/57.50/55.88, WiC 51.28/51.00/53.57. Declared in rows_left_out, but it bears directly on the V6 verdict.
EusTrivia category scores and EusExams category scores across Latxa sizes; all rise with size.

record.verdict_notes: The record's baselines are same-size Llama 2 models, which measure the continued-pretraining effect rather than scale. For V6, the proper comparison is across Latxa sizes. Scale is confounded with base model, but the Llama 2 bases share training data and the continued-pretraining token count is fixed at 10B for all sizes. The evidence is three points with no uncertainty, so it is weak support at best. The authors' reading of Kaplan et al. as predicting a data bottleneck is itself debatable, since Kaplan et al. find larger models are more sample-efficient.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out loss versus parameters, tokens, and compute; power-law form and range.
Prediction of larger-run loss from laws fitted on smaller runs.
Compute-optimal parameter/token allocation and its trend with compute.
Effects of architecture depth, width, or other details at fixed parameter count.
Power-law loss scaling in other modalities or training regimes.
The study measures downstream accuracy across three sizes, but does not fit a predictive relationship, test extrapolation, or relate downstream results to held-out pretraining loss.
Dependence of fitted exponents or compute-optimal allocation on fitting choices, and departures from a single power law.
